title: Why does gRPC rely on HTTP/2 instead of HTTP/1.1, and what breaks with HTTP/1.1 (no multiplexing/streaming/binary)?
shortTitle: Why does gRPC rely on HTTP/2 instead of HTTP/1.1, and what breaks with HTTP/1.1 (no multiplexing/streaming/binary)?
keyPoints: gRPC depends on HTTP/2's stream multiplexing to run many concurrent RPCs over one TCP connection without head-of-line blocking.
HTTP/2's full-duplex bidirectional streaming enables gRPC's server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional call types.
HTTP/2's binary framing layer matches gRPC's binary Protocol Buffers payloads and length-prefixed message framing.
gRPC sends the final status code in HTTP/2 trailers after the response body, which HTTP/1.1 does not support reliably.
HTTP/2's HPACK header compression reduces overhead for the many small metadata headers gRPC uses per call.
This HTTP/2 dependency is why browsers cannot speak native gRPC and need gRPC-Web with a translating proxy.
An HTTP/1.1-only proxy or incorrectly terminating load balancer silently breaks gRPC multiplexing and streaming.

s1_definition.oneliner: gRPC needs HTTP/2's multiplexing, bidirectional streaming, binary framing, and trailers; HTTP/1.1 lacks all of these, so gRPC's streaming and concurrency model cannot run on it.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Stream multiplexing** – HTTP/2 carries many concurrent, independent request/response streams over one TCP connection, which gRPC uses for concurrent RPCs without opening many connections.
- **Bidirectional streaming** – HTTP/2 supports full-duplex data flow in both directions on the same stream, enabling gRPC's server, client, and bidirectional streaming calls.
- **Binary framing** – HTTP/2's binary frame layer matches gRPC's binary Protocol Buffers and length-prefixed message framing for efficient transport.
- **Trailers** – gRPC sends the final status code (`grpc-status`) in HTTP/2 trailing headers after the response body, which HTTP/1.1 does not support reliably.
- **HPACK compression** – Header compression reduces per-call overhead for gRPC's metadata headers.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the line between the transfers desk and the accounts desk at National Bank of India. HTTP/1.1 is like a single phone line where you must finish one whole call before starting the next, and you cannot talk and listen continuously at the same time. HTTP/2 is like a modern switchboard on one wire that carries dozens of calls at once, each independent, and lets both sides talk simultaneously. gRPC was designed for busy, streaming, two-way conversations between desks, so it needs the switchboard. On the old single-call line, its streaming and concurrent-calls features simply cannot happen.

```text
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│      HTTP/2 Features gRPC Depends On              │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────┐                 │
│  │  Stream Multiplexing         │                 │
│  │  Stream 1: Transfer call     │                 │
│  │  Stream 3: Balance call      │  ONE TCP conn   │
│  │  Stream 5: Statement stream  │                 │
│  │  Stream 7: Fraud check       │                 │
│  └──────────────────────────────┘                 │
│                                                   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────┐                 │
│  │  Bidirectional Streaming     │                 │
│  │  Client → DATA DATA DATA     │                 │
│  │  Server → DATA DATA DATA     │  same stream    │
│  │  Server → TRAILERS (status)  │                 │
│  └──────────────────────────────┘                 │
│                                                   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────┐                 │
│  │  Binary Framing              │                 │
│  │  [length][type][stream-id]   │                 │
│  │  [protobuf payload]          │  compact        │
│  └──────────────────────────────┘                 │
│                                                   │
│  HTTP/1.1 lacks ALL of these:                     │
│  - No multiplexing (one req at a time)            │
│  - No bidirectional streaming                     │
│  - Text-based headers (no HPACK)                  │
│  - No reliable trailers                           │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
gRPC relies on HTTP/2 because its core features map directly onto HTTP/2 capabilities that HTTP/1.1 does not have. HTTP/2 gives stream multiplexing, so many independent RPCs run concurrently over one connection without blocking each other. It gives full-duplex bidirectional streaming, so a single logical call can carry a sequence of messages in both directions. It is binary by design, matching gRPC's Protocol Buffers and length-prefixed framing. And it supports trailers, which gRPC uses to send the final status code after a streamed body.

On HTTP/1.1, several things break. There is no real multiplexing, so a connection handles one request and response at a time, defeating gRPC's concurrent-calls model. There is no true full-duplex bidirectional streaming, so client-streaming and bidirectional calls cannot be represented. There are no reliable trailers, so the status-after-stream mechanism fails. And the text-oriented framing is mismatched with gRPC's binary payloads.

In banking work at National Bank of India a server-streaming statement feed used one request for Rajesh's account to yield a continuous stream of transaction entries on a single call, with the final status delivered in trailers. That pattern only exists because of HTTP/2 streaming and trailers. At the same time the transfer service fires many concurrent account calls over one multiplexed channel without them blocking each other.

The HTTP/2 dependency is exactly why browsers cannot speak native gRPC, since they do not expose raw HTTP/2 framing to JavaScript, so gRPC-Web with a translating proxy like Envoy is required. It is also why HTTP/2 must be verified on every hop, because an older HTTP/1.1-only proxy or an incorrectly terminating load balancer silently breaks multiplexing and streaming.

Remember one sentence: gRPC needs HTTP/2's multiplexing, bidirectional streaming, binary framing, and trailers, and HTTP/1.1 lacks every one of them, so gRPC's concurrency and streaming model cannot run on it.
